task: Extract adversarial negative-sample construction methodology from three papers cited by Butoi et al. 2024 ("Training Neural Networks as Recognizers of Formal Languages", the FLaRe paper this repo implements), and compare each against FLaRe's own K-edit approach.

flare_citation_context.source: Butoi, Khalighinejad, Svete, Valvoda, Cotterell, DuSell. "Training Neural Networks as Recognizers of Formal Languages." arXiv:2411.07107 / ICLR 2025.
flare_citation_context.verbatim_quote: Prior work, therefore, typically uses language-specific rules to generate adversarial negative samples (Weiss et al., 2018b; Bhattamishra et al., 2024; Someya et al., 2024). To keep our methodology more general, the other half of the time, we propose a perturbed negative example by sampling a positive example and perturbing it with random edits (cf. Weiss et al., 2018a).
flare_citation_context.note: FLaRe's bibliography actually splits Weiss et al. 2018 into TWO entries: 2018a = "On the Practical Computational Power of Finite Precision RNNs for Language Recognition" (the paper the user means by 'Weiss et al. 2018 on RNN language recognition'), cited as the INSPIRATION for FLaRe's own random-edit perturbation methodology; 2018b = "Learning to Parse and its Applications for Code" (a different paper, cited alongside Bhattamishra 2024 and Someya 2024 as an example of the language-specific-rules camp). This JSON covers 2018a per the user's explicit framing ("RNN language recognition"), since that is both the paper the user asked for AND the one whose actual negative-sampling methodology is analyzed below (2018b was not fetched -- it is a code-parsing paper, off-topic for this comparison).

flare_own_method_for_reference.construction: Two-part mixed strategy per negative example: (1) 50% of the time, a UNIFORM-RANDOM negative: sample length n uniformly from [n_min, n_max], then sample a string uniformly from the full alphabet Sigma^n. (2) 50% of the time, a PERTURBED negative: sample a genuine positive example, sample the number of edits K from a geometric distribution heavily favoring small K, then iteratively apply K uniformly-sampled edits, each independently chosen to be a single-symbol insertion, replacement, or deletion at a uniformly-random position.
flare_own_method_for_reference.generality: GENERIC / language-agnostic. The edit operation vocabulary (insert/replace/delete a single symbol) is defined purely in terms of the alphabet and requires no per-language design -- the same three-operation K-edit procedure is applied unchanged across every task in the FLaRe benchmark (arithmetic, marker, grammar, navigation tasks alike). This project's own 'fix' experiments (this session's work) additionally replace the K-edit half with explicit swap/bit-flip constructions per task specifically because K-edit was found to under-cover the truly hard cases -- but that is a distinct, later refinement layered on top of FLaRe's original generic method, not part of the original FLaRe paper being compared here.

papers.citation: Gail Weiss, Yoav Goldberg, Eran Yahav. "On the Practical Computational Power of Finite Precision RNNs for Language Recognition." ACL 2018 (Short Papers), pp. 740-745.
papers.source_verified: Fetched and read the full ACL Anthology PDF (P18-2117.pdf) directly.
papers.paper_topic: Theoretical + empirical study of the computational power of finite-precision RNN variants (SRNN, IRNN/ReLU-RNN, GRU, LSTM) restricted to linear-time, input-bound computation. Shows LSTM and IRNN can implement unbounded per-dimension counting (making them at least as strong as k-counter machines / SKCMs), while SRNN and GRU cannot. Empirically trains LSTM/GRU on the counting languages a^n b^n and a^n b^n c^n to confirm the theory.

exact_construction_method.training_and_dev_negatives: Verbatim (footnote 6, p.744): 'Positive examples are generated by sampling n in the desired range. For negative examples we sample 2 or 3 n values independently, and ensuring at least one of them differs from the others.' I.e. for a^n b^n, sample n_a and n_b INDEPENDENTLY (rejecting if n_a == n_b) instead of requiring n_a == n_b == n; for a^n b^n c^n, sample n_a, n_b, n_c independently with the same non-equality constraint.
exact_construction_method.held_out_test_set_negatives: Verbatim (p.744): for a^n b^n, test words of the form a^(n+i) b^(n+j) where n ~ rand(0,200) and i,j ~ rand(-2,2) independently; for a^n b^n c^n, words a^(n+i) b^(n+j) c^(n+k) where n ~ rand(0,150) and i,j,k ~ rand(-2,2) independently. This produces NEAR-MISS negatives (small independent per-block count offsets around a shared base n), a harder/more targeted test distribution than the train/dev negatives' fully-independent count sampling.
exact_construction_method.positive_construction: Sample n (or n plus small per-block offsets) directly from the target range; the string is built deterministically from the exact-count definition of the language (e.g., n copies of 'a' followed by n copies of 'b').

papers.language_specific_or_generic: LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC (narrow: counting languages only). The entire construction hinges on the target language having an explicit, identifiable PER-SYMBOL-BLOCK COUNT structure (a^n b^n requires count(a)==count(b); a^n b^n c^n requires count(a)==count(b)==count(c)) -- negatives are generated by breaking exactly that count-equality relationship, either fully independently (train/dev) or via small correlated offsets around a shared n (test). This construction has no direct analogue for languages without a symbol-counting structure (e.g. a marker/copy task, a grammar-parsing task, a navigation task) -- it does not generalize the way an edit-distance-based procedure does.
papers.evaluation_paradigm: Direct binary recognizer evaluation (f(RNN(w)) in {0,1}), trained via backpropagation to 100% dev accuracy, then measured on the held-out near-miss test set plus longer-length generalization sweeps. Same fundamental recognizer-evaluation paradigm as FLaRe (unlike Someya et al. 2024, see below).
papers.difference_from_flare_k_edit: FLaRe's K-edit is a SINGLE generic procedure (bounded-K random insert/replace/delete) applied identically to every language in the benchmark, requiring no per-language analysis. Weiss et al. 2018a's negative construction instead exploits language-specific arithmetic structure (independent/near-miss per-block count perturbation) that only makes sense for counting languages with an explicit block-count definition -- it cannot be mechanically reused for FLaRe's marker-family, grammar-family, or navigation tasks without inventing a new, per-language perturbation rule each time. This is exactly the pattern FLaRe's own paper describes itself as generalizing away from. Also notable: FLaRe's own K-edit citation ('cf. Weiss et al., 2018a') credits this paper only for the general SPIRIT of perturbing near a positive example, not for the specific per-block-count mechanism -- the two methods are not the same procedure, only related in motivation.

papers.citation: Satwik Bhattamishra, Michael Hahn, Phil Blunsom, Varun Kanade. "Separations in the Representational Capabilities of Transformers and Recurrent Architectures." NeurIPS 2024 / arXiv:2406.09347.
papers.source_verified: Fetched and read the full arXiv PDF (main text sections 1-7 plus Appendix H, 'Empirical Analysis: Additional Details and Experiments', including H.1 Bounded Dycks and H.2 String Equality) directly.
papers.paper_topic: Primarily a THEORETICAL paper proving representational-SIZE separations between Transformers and recurrent models (RNNs/LSTMs/SSMs) on Index Lookup, Bounded Dyck recognition, String Equality/Disjointness, and Nearest-Neighbor/associative-recall tasks -- e.g. one-layer Transformers of logarithmic width can do Index Lookup while any recurrent model needs linear width; constant-size RNNs can recognize bounded Dyck languages while one-layer Transformers need linear size. Supplements the theory with an empirical section (Section 6 + Appendix H) training real models on these tasks at practical sizes.

exact_construction_method.bounded_dyck_negatives: Verbatim (Appendix H.1, p.35): 'To generate negative examples, we first sample a positive example and then corrupt some of the symbols in the string. For strings of length N, we first sample a number k = 1,...,N/10 uniformly at random and then pick k different indices uniformly at random. For each of those positions, with probability 1/2, we swap the types of brackets, e.g. round '(' to square '[', and with probability 1/2 we switch open brackets to closing brackets (or vice versa). There is a very small probability that after the corruption the resulting string will still be a valid well-balanced string of depth at most 2, in which case we redo the corruption again.' Positives themselves are generated by a bounded-depth-respecting random walk (iterate N-2 steps, track current bracket-nesting depth, constrain choices to keep depth < 2), not sampled from a grammar directly.
exact_construction_method.string_equality_negatives_two_shortcut_p: Eq-random: second half of the string is an independently-uniform-random string of the same length as the first half (differs from the first half with high probability ~ 1 - 2^(-k/2)). Eq-one: second half is set EQUAL to the first half, then exactly one position is changed to a different symbol.
exact_construction_method.string_equality_shortcut_problem_explici: Verbatim (Appendix H.2, p.36): 'One thing to note is that both of the experimental setups described above can be solved using some form of shortcuts... Even if it stores the first few elements, then with high probability it can determine the label of the string correctly [Eq-random]... a recurrent model can solve it perfectly by just maintaining a dictionary of the counts of each symbol in the vocabulary [Eq-one, since a single substitution necessarily changes at least one symbol's count]. To rule out such phenomena, we adopt the next character prediction setting.'
exact_construction_method.next_character_prediction_workaround: Rather than fix the negative-construction methodology for binary classification, the authors abandon binary classification for the equality task entirely and reformulate it as next-token/next-character prediction (multi-label valid-continuation prediction at every prefix), which sidesteps needing negative EXAMPLES at all for this task.

papers.language_specific_or_generic: LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC for Bounded Dyck: the corruption operation vocabulary (bracket-TYPE swap, e.g. '(' -> '[' ; open/close FLIP) is only meaningful for bracket-matching languages -- it presupposes the alphabet has a bracket-type dimension and an open/close dimension, neither of which exists in most of FLaRe's tasks (e.g. binary arithmetic, marker-copy, navigation). Structurally the RANDOM-K-POSITIONS sampling scaffold (choose k in [1, N/10], pick k random indices, corrupt each) is procedurally similar in SHAPE to FLaRe's K-edit (also 'choose a small K, apply K random local corruptions'), but the actual per-position corruption OPERATIONS are hand-designed for the bracket alphabet, not generic single-symbol insert/replace/delete over an arbitrary alphabet. For String Equality, the paper does not solve the negative-construction problem at all for the classification setting -- it explicitly documents both of its own negative-construction attempts as shortcut-exploitable and switches evaluation paradigms instead.
papers.evaluation_paradigm: Direct binary recognizer evaluation for Index Lookup and Bounded Dyck (same family as FLaRe); switches to next-character/next-token PREDICTION (not binary classification) for String Equality specifically, to avoid the acknowledged shortcut problem.
papers.difference_from_flare_k_edit: Bounded-Dyck's construction shares FLaRe K-edit's high-level SHAPE (small random K, K randomly-placed local corruptions) but not its GENERALITY -- the corruption vocabulary is hand-designed per language (bracket-type/open-close operations exist only because Dyck languages have that structure) rather than defined generically over any alphabet via insert/replace/delete. More importantly, this paper's String Equality experiments are the clearest documented case in this comparison of the EXACT failure mode FLaRe's K-edit approach (and this project's own 'fix' experiments) are designed to avoid: the authors tried two negative-construction schemes, found BOTH exploitable via trivial shortcuts (position-count / symbol-count dictionaries), and rather than design a harder, shortcut-resistant negative construction (which is what FLaRe's K-edit -- and this project's swap/bit-flip 'fix' constructions -- attempt to do), they sidestepped the problem by changing the task formulation away from binary classification entirely. FLaRe (and this project) instead keep binary classification and try to make the NEGATIVES themselves harder to shortcut.

papers.citation: Taiga Someya, Ryo Yoshida, Yohei Oseki. "Targeted Syntactic Evaluation on the Chomsky Hierarchy." LREC-COLING 2024, pp. 15595-15605.
papers.source_verified: Fetched and read the full ACL Anthology PDF (2024.lrec-main.1356.pdf) directly, including Section 3.2 'Data Generation' and 3.2.3 'Generating negative examples' with Table 2 (worked examples).
papers.paper_topic: Proposes a BLiMP-style Targeted Syntactic Evaluation using four SYNTHETIC formal languages, each hand-designed to abstract one natural-language syntactic phenomenon at a specific level of the Chomsky hierarchy: (1) (Adj)^n NP (regular; models unbounded adjective stacking), (2) NP^n VP^n (context-free; models embedded sentences without NP-VP agreement, as in Japanese), (3) Nested Dependency (context-free; models NP-VP number agreement under center-embedding, as in English 'The dogs that the cat chases bark'), (4) Cross Serial Dependency (context-sensitive; models crossing dependencies as in Swiss German). Trains LSTM, Transformer-LM, and Stack-RNN language models and evaluates via minimal-pair probability comparison. Finds all three architectures capture (Adj)^n NP, but none correctly recognize Nested or Cross-Serial Dependency, and LSTM/Transformer also fail NP^n VP^n.

exact_construction_method.adj_n_np: Verbatim (Sec 3.2.3): 'We generate a negative example by replacing k ~ U(1, l-1) occurrences of Adj's with NP's in a corresponding positive example of length l.' (i.e. substitute a random NUMBER of Adj tokens with NP tokens, breaking the required 'all Adjs then one NP' pattern.)
exact_construction_method.np_n_vp_n: Verbatim: 'We generate a negative example by either adding or removing a single occurrence of NP or VP.' (i.e. a single insertion or deletion, breaking the required matched NP-count == VP-count.)
exact_construction_method.nested_and_cross_serial_dependency: Verbatim: 'We generate a negative example by selecting two positions within the NP or VP and swapping their occurrences in a corresponding positive example... We create negative examples by breaking dependencies between non-terminals because we are interested in whether the language models can successfully capture the dependencies between non-terminals.' (i.e. a SWAP of two positions within the same block, preserving surface token COUNTS but breaking the index-to-index dependency pairing -- structurally identical in spirit to this project's own swap-based 'fix' hard-negative constructions, e.g. marked-copy/odds-first/repeat-01/stack-manipulation.)
exact_construction_method.minimal_pair_evaluation: Each formal language additionally instantiated at 5 different terminal-symbol-set sizes T in {5,10,50,100,500}, generating 110,000 samples per language (90k train / 10k in-distribution test / 10k out-of-distribution longer-length test), giving 24 total formal-language variants tested.

papers.language_specific_or_generic: LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC, explicitly and by design: FOUR ENTIRELY DIFFERENT negative-construction rules for the FOUR formal-language types, chosen specifically to isolate each language's own defining structural constraint (Adj-count-vs-NP-position for the regular language; NP-count==VP-count for the context-free counting language; NP_i-to-VP_i INDEX PAIRING for the two dependency languages). The paper does not claim or attempt a single shared negative-construction procedure across its four languages -- each rule is hand-derived from that language's own grammar to targetedly break exactly the syntactic property being tested (paralleling this project's own general practice of deriving a bespoke swap/bit-flip construction per FLaRe task, rather than reusing one generic rule).
papers.evaluation_paradigm: NOT a binary recognizer classifier. This is the one paper of the three that departs from FLaRe's own evaluation setup entirely: models are trained as LANGUAGE MODELS (next-token prediction over Sigma), then evaluated via minimal-pair PROBABILITY COMPARISON (does the LM assign P(positive sentence) > P(negative sentence)?), i.e. the BLiMP paradigm (Warstadt et al. 2020), not string classification. This mirrors exactly the mismatch Butoi et al. 2024 (FLaRe) identify as their own core motivation -- FLaRe's introduction argues that formal-language theory is about RECOGNIZERS (direct string-membership classifiers), and that evaluating via LM-probability comparison (as Someya et al. 2024 do) is a mismatch with that theory that FLaRe's own binary-classifier training methodology is built to correct.
papers.difference_from_flare_k_edit: Two layers of difference. (1) Construction: Someya et al. 2024 use FOUR distinct, hand-crafted operations (substitution-of-a-random-count, single insertion/deletion, and positional swap) individually derived from each target language's own grammar, versus FLaRe's ONE generic operation set (bounded-K insert/replace/delete over the raw alphabet) applied unchanged to every language in the benchmark. Someya's swap-based rule for the two dependency languages is actually the closest of all three papers' methods to this project's own 'fix' hard-negative constructions (e.g. marked-copy/odds-first/repeat-01's differing-adjacent-value swaps) -- both exploit a swap to preserve surface counts while breaking positional/order correctness -- but Someya's swap rule is still bespoke per language, not reused verbatim as a single general-purpose procedure the way FLaRe's K-edit is. (2) Evaluation paradigm: Someya et al. 2024 evaluate via LM minimal-pair probability comparison, not direct binary classification -- a more fundamental methodological divergence from FLaRe than either Weiss et al. 2018a or Bhattamishra et al. 2024, both of which (like FLaRe) train and evaluate models as direct string recognizers.

cross_paper_summary.shared_pattern_across_all_three: All three papers construct negative examples via HAND-DESIGNED, PER-LANGUAGE (or per-language-family) corruption rules that exploit that specific language's own defining structural invariant -- count-equality for Weiss's counting languages, bracket-type/open-close identity for Bhattamishra's Dyck languages, and count/index-pairing invariants for Someya's four syntactic-phenomenon languages -- rather than a single alphabet-agnostic procedure. This directly substantiates FLaRe's own characterization of them as a group: 'prior work... typically uses language-specific rules to generate adversarial negative samples.'
cross_paper_summary.flare_generic_alternative: FLaRe's K-edit avoids per-language design entirely by defining negatives purely in terms of the ALPHABET (any single-symbol insertion, replacement, or deletion, applied K times with K drawn from a shared geometric distribution), letting the SAME procedure run unmodified across FLaRe's full task suite (arithmetic, marker/copy, grammar, navigation families alike) without requiring a human to identify each new language's specific structural invariant first.

closest_and_furthest_relatives_to_flare.structurally_closest_to_k_edit: Bhattamishra et al. 2024's Bounded-Dyck construction (same 'small random K, K randomly-placed local corruptions' scaffold), though its corruption ops are bracket-specific, not alphabet-generic.
closest_and_furthest_relatives_to_flare.conceptually_closest_to_this_projects_ow: Someya et al. 2024's swap-based construction for Nested/Cross-Serial Dependency (positional swap preserving surface counts, breaking only the index-pairing/order) -- structurally the same idea this project's own 'fix' experiments use throughout this session (marked-copy, odds-first, repeat-01, stack-manipulation all use a differing-value swap to preserve trivial shortcut features while breaking the true target).
closest_and_furthest_relatives_to_flare.furthest_from_flare_methodologically: Someya et al. 2024 overall, because of its evaluation-paradigm divergence (LM minimal-pairs, not binary classification) on top of its language-specific construction -- and Bhattamishra et al. 2024's String Equality experiments, because they document giving up on constructing shortcut-resistant negatives at all for that task and changing the task formulation instead, whereas FLaRe (and this project) treat 'the negatives are shortcut-exploitable' as a problem to fix via better negative construction, not a reason to abandon binary classification.
